reading.body:
Competitive intelligence in life sciences now runs on AI platforms that fuse pipeline, trial, safety and business data, with Causaly launching an application built on its biomedical knowledge graph.

The pattern is consolidation of sources that analysts previously read separately. Pipeline status, trial results, safety signals and commercial signals are joined in one knowledge graph, which is what lets a team spot a competitor's shift early rather than reconstruct it weeks later from scattered filings and press releases.

The division of labor matters more than the automation. AI widens coverage and speeds alerts, and analysts stay responsible for the conclusions shared with leadership. That is a governance choice as much as a technical one, and it is the part a commercial team should read closely.

The data covers one named platform and one launch. It does not say how many competitors are tracked, how the knowledge graph is built or updated, what the application costs, or whether any commercial team has reported a decision changed by it. Nothing here speaks to compute, buildings or power, so no claim about the grid can be drawn from it.

explainer:
Competitive intelligence teams track rival companies' pipelines, trial starts and results, regulatory decisions, launches, pricing and deals, then brief leadership on what it means. The volume of sources, registries, publications, conference abstracts, filings and news, makes this a strong fit for AI.

Platforms built on biomedical knowledge graphs link entities such as targets, drugs, diseases and companies, so analysts can ask questions across sources and get alerts when something changes. AI widens coverage and speeds detection; judgement about significance and strategy stays with analysts, who should verify key facts before they reach decision makers.

What AI adds to competitive intelligence

Competitive intelligence teams in life sciences track clinical trial registries, regulatory filings, patents, conference abstracts, earnings calls, press releases and job postings to anticipate what rivals will do. The volume has outgrown manual reading. Language models now do the first pass: extracting trial design changes, flagging new indications in patent claims, summarising what an executive said about a pipeline asset, and noticing when a competitor starts hiring for a launch. The analyst then verifies and interprets.

Where it is most useful

The best returns come from structured public sources that change often: trial registries, where an enrolment change or endpoint change signals strategy; regulatory databases, where approvals and advisory committee schedules are posted; and patent offices, where claims reveal where a competitor is investing. Linking these to the company's own forecasts turns intelligence into a decision about timing, pricing or trial design.

The discipline required

AI makes it easy to produce confident summaries of thin evidence. A good programme records the source of every claim, distinguishes what a competitor said from what the model inferred, and avoids anything that crosses into improper collection of non public information. Competition law also limits how intelligence can be used, especially around pricing. The tool speeds the reading; the judgement and the ethics stay with the team.
